summary:
The answers can never be larger than `n + k`: n numbers can block at most n of the values
`1 … n + k`, so at least k of them are free. That bound turns the problem into marking flags in
an array of size `n + k` and reading off the first k empty ones, O(n + k) with no hashing.

question.md:
List the `k` smallest positive integers (1, 2, 3, …) that don't appear in `nums`, in increasing
order.

- **Only positive answers.** 0 and negative numbers in `nums` never block anything, because
  they aren't candidates.
- **Repeats block a value once.** Two 3s still only remove 3.
- **Answers can go past the largest number in the list.** For `nums = [2, 3, 4]` and k = 3 the
  answer is `[1, 5, 6]`: after 1, the next free values are above 4.
- **Huge values in `nums` (up to 10⁹)** are irrelevant unless they fall among the first few
  free numbers, which they can't, as we'll see.
- **Size:** n and k each up to 10⁵.

think.md:
Take `nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]` and `k = 3`. Counting up by hand: 1 ✓ taken, 2 ✓, 3 ✓,
4 ✓, **5** free, **6** free, 7 ✓, 8 ✓, **9** free. Answer `[5, 6, 9]`.

The doing-it-by-hand method is already the algorithm: count up from 1 and skip what's taken. The
only question is how quickly you can ask "is x taken?", and how far up you might have to go.

**How far?** Look at the values `1 … n + k`. There are n + k of them, and the list has only n
numbers, so at most n of those values are taken. That leaves at least k free values inside
`1 … n + k`. So the counting never needs to pass `n + k`, and any number in `nums` bigger than
that can be ignored.

think.caption: With 8 numbers and k = 3, everything happens inside 1 … 11, and the first three blanks are the answer.

think.md:
That bound is what lets a plain array replace a hash set: index `v` of an array of size `n + k`
answers "is v taken?".

approaches.title: Count up and scan the list each time

idea.md:
Try candidates 1, 2, 3, … in order. For each one, scan `nums`. If it's not there, it's
missing: add it to the answer. Stop once you have k.

At most n + k candidates are tried (by the bound above), and each scan costs n.

build: Start with an empty answer and `x = 1`.
While the answer has fewer than k numbers: scan `nums` for `x`; if absent, append `x`.

lines.text: The answer so far, and the first candidate, 1.

notes.java: We know the answer has exactly k numbers, so allocate them up front and fill with `found`.
notes.c: Room for exactly k answers; `found` counts how many are filled.

lines.text: Keep going until k missing numbers are collected.
Look for `x` in the whole list. Not there means it's missing.
Move on to the next candidate.
The answers were found in increasing order, so no sorting is needed.

notes.c: Report the length through `returnSize`; the caller frees `out`.

complexity.md: **Time O((n + k) · n):** up to n + k candidates, each scanning n numbers (≈ 2 × 10¹⁰ at the limits). **Space O(1)** beyond the answer.

steps.text: 5: scan the whole list, not there. Missing #1.
6: scan the whole list, not there. Missing #2.
9: scan the whole list, not there. Missing #3.

walk.title: Try 1, 2, 3, … and scan the whole list for each one.

limits.md: Every membership question costs a full scan. Store the numbers somewhere with O(1) lookups and the scans disappear.

approaches.title: Hash set, then count up

idea.md:
Put every number in a hash set once. Then count up from 1 exactly as before, but each
"is x taken?" is now an O(1) lookup.

build: Count `x` up from 1, appending each `x` not in the set, until there are k answers.

lines.text: C has no hash set, so here's a minimal one: a slot holds a key and an in-use flag, and `slotOf` scrambles a key into a starting slot (multiply by a large odd constant, keep the high bits).
Every number goes into the set once; repeats collapse.

notes.c: The table is a power of two at least 2n in size. Each number probes forward from its slot until it finds itself or an empty slot, then claims it.

lines.text: Candidates 1, 2, 3, … until k answers are collected.
An O(1) average lookup replaces the scan.

notes.c: Probe from `x`'s slot; reaching an empty slot means `x` was never added.

lines.text: Answers come out in increasing order.

notes.c: Free the table and report the length.

complexity.md: **Time O(n + k)** on average: n inserts and at most n + k lookups. **Space O(n)** for the set.

steps.text: The set holds every number once: {1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8}.

walk.title: Put the numbers in a hash set, then count up from 1 with O(1) checks.

limits.md:
Fast enough, but the set stores numbers that can never matter (negatives, zeros, anything
above n + k), and hash lookups are O(1) only on average. Knowing that every answer is at
most n + k lets us use plain array indices instead.

approaches.title: Flags for 1 … n + k

idea.md:
Every answer is at most `n + k` (n numbers can block at most n of the values
`1 … n + k`). So make a boolean array `present` of size `n + k + 1`, flag each number of
`nums` that falls in `1 … n + k`, and ignore the rest. Then walk `1, 2, …` and collect the
first k unflagged values.

build: Let `limit = n + k` and make `present` with `limit + 1` falses.
For each `v` in `nums` with `1 ≤ v ≤ limit`, set `present[v] = true`.
Walk `x` from 1 upward, appending every `x` with `present[x]` false, until k are found. It can't run past `limit`.

lines.text: The answers all lie in `1 … n + k`, so that's the only range worth tracking. One flag per value (index 0 is unused, so index `v` means value `v`).
Flag each number that could block an answer. Zeros, negatives and anything above `limit` can't, so they're skipped (and they'd be out of the array's range anyway).
Collect unflagged values in increasing order until there are k of them. Because at least k values in `1 … limit` are unflagged, `x` never runs past `limit`.
Return the k smallest missing positives.

notes.c: Free the flags and report the length; the caller frees `out`.

complexity.md:
**Time O(n + k):** one pass to flag, at most n + k steps to read. No hashing, so it's
O(1) per step in the worst case, not just on average.

**Space O(n + k)** for the flags (2 × 10⁵ booleans at most).

steps.text: n = 8, k = 3. Only the numbers 1 … 11 can matter. Make 11 empty flags.
Read the flags left to right; the first 3 empty ones are [5, 6, 9].

walk.title: The answers can't go past n + k = 11. Mark which of 1 … 11 appear, then read off the first k gaps.

takeaways.md:
- **Bound the answer first.** "n items can block at most n values" tells you every answer lies in
  `1 … n + k`, and a small known range means an array can replace a hash set.
- Values outside the useful range are noise: skip them before indexing.
- For the classic k = 1 version, the same bound is `1 … n + 1`, and if you're allowed to
  rearrange the input you can even do it in O(1) extra space by parking each value `v` at index
  `v − 1` (cyclic sort). See **First Missing Ticket**.
